Louis-Antoine de Saint-Just. Born in 1767, this young radical revolutionary emerged as one of the revolution's most feared figures. He had a gift for oratory and an uncompromising vision of revolutionary virtue. He became a key architect of the Reign of Terror on the Committee of Public Safety alongside Robespierre from 1793 to 1794. As a dominant force on the Committee, he signed arrest warrants and called for purges of suspected enemies. He delivered influential speeches calling for the execution of King Louis XVI, framing it as necessary to eliminate the revolution's enemies. He orchestrated the elimination of the Enragés, the radical extremists, and the Hébertists, and the Dantonists, using terror as an instrument of revolutionary purification. In February and March of 1794, he authored the Ventôse Decrees, which attempted to redistribute the property of émigrés and suspects to the poor, embodying radical redistributive ideals. But when he and Robespierre threatened further purges after June 1794, even their allies turned against them. During the Thermidorian Reaction of July 1794, Saint-Just fell from power alongside Robespierre. He was arrested without support from the Convention. He was executed by guillotine on July 28, 1794, the ninth of Thermidor. He made no attempt to defend himself or recant his beliefs.
